hook.text: Slamming the brakes on ice used to mean locked wheels, no steering, and pure terror.

buildup.text: A locked wheel slides instead of rolling. Sliding tires have far less grip than rolling ones.

discovery.text: ABS uses sensors to detect which wheels are about to lock, then rapidly pulses the brakes on and off.

twist.text: It pumps the brakes up to 15 times per second—faster than any human foot could ever manage.

climax.text: The result: the tires keep rolling, you keep steering, and stopping distance shrinks on slippery roads.

punchline.text: ABS doesn't stop faster—it lets you steer while stopping.

quiz.question: What does ABS primarily help you do?

details.summary: Anti-lock braking systems rapidly pulse the brakes on and off during hard stops to prevent wheel lockup, allowing the driver to maintain steering control while stopping as quickly as possible.
details.whyItMatters: Locked wheels slide uncontrollably. ABS keeps tires rotating just enough to maintain grip, letting drivers steer around obstacles during emergency braking and reducing crash severity.
takeaways: ABS modulates brake pressure up to 15 times per second
It prevents wheel lockup to maintain steering ability
ABS is now mandatory on all new cars in most countries

faq.question: Should I pump the brakes if my car has ABS?
faq.answer: No. With ABS, press the brake pedal firmly and hold it. The system pumps far faster than any human can. Pumping manually actually interferes with ABS operation and increases stopping distance.

faq.question: Does ABS always shorten stopping distances?
faq.answer: Not always. On loose gravel or deep snow, locked wheels can dig in and stop sooner. On paved roads, ABS almost always shortens stopping distances while preserving steering control.
